tip: A negative command keeps the pronoun in front: ne les ouvre pas. Flip to a positive order and it jumps behind with a hyphen: ouvre-les.
Positive commands tack pronouns on with hyphens, and me turns into moi: donne-le-moi – the thing (le) first, the person (moi) second.
Chercher already means 'look for', so the 'for' is built in – it takes a plain object: il la cherche partout, never 'chercher pour'.
You phone TO someone in French: téléphoner à quelqu'un. That à becomes lui – tu lui téléphones, not 'tu la téléphones'.
Object pronouns land BEFORE the verb: il me comprend = he understands me, literally 'he me understands'.
Avoir besoin DE hides a de, so 'need it' brings the it back as en: j'en ai besoin = literally 'I have need OF it'.
Depuis takes the present where English needs 'have been': tu la regardes depuis cinq minutes = you've been watching for five minutes.
No 'will' required – French often uses the plain present for a set plan: je te rappelle ce soir = I'll call you back tonight.
See someone do something = voir + a bare infinitive: je la vois partir. La is who you see, partir is the action, no 'to'.
Slip a direct object before avoir and the past participle agrees: les a lus grows an s. Drop the les and it stays lu.
Sortir builds its past with être, not avoir, so the participle agrees with the subject: elle est sortie – that e marks 'she'.
Par marks the means or channel, like English 'by' or 'via': par courriel = by email. Same in par téléphone, par la poste.
English says 'wants me to go', but French won't cross two subjects with a plain infinitive: veut que j'aille (from aller), subjunctive.
You aren't right in French, you HAVE reason: avoir raison. Being right always uses a form of avoir – tu aies raison here.
English can drop 'some', French can't: 'do you eat often?' still needs en standing in for it – tu en manges souvent ?
Leur here is the pronoun 'to them', not the possessive leurs – so it never takes an s: il leur a raconté une histoire, plural yet still leur.
Reprendre at the table means take another helping; en stands for the food: elle en a repris deux fois = she had seconds twice.
Two object pronouns stack before the verb, me then le, and le clips to l' before a vowel: elle ne me l'a jamais dit.
Surprise about something already done takes the past subjunctive: que personne n'ait remarqué – ait, not the everyday 'a'.
Quirk: a preceding en never makes the participle agree. Elle en a commandé cinq stays commandé, no s – unlike les a commandés.
